Case overview

Why this project exists

Cure started as a response to a D&AD New Blood Awards live brief, sponsored by 21GRAMS, on designing for myopia and screen-time behavior change. I took it on solo, treating it as a proper research-led project rather than a portfolio exercise, even though it was never submitted to the awards.

The rest of this page walks through the research I grounded it in, the competitive landscape it sits inside, and the concept it resolved into. Real screens and final visuals are still being dropped in, so a few sections below are marked as placeholders for now.

The brief

A live brief about attention, not eyesight

The brief's framing was blunt: screens are reshaping how often and how intensely we use our eyes, and myopia rates in young people are climbing alongside it. The ask wasn't a medical device, it was a companion product that helps someone notice the strain building up before it compounds into something worse.

That framing mattered for scope. It ruled out a purely clinical tool and pointed toward something that had to compete for attention against the very screens it was trying to protect people from, which became the central design tension for the whole project.

The hardest constraint wasn't the eye-health content. It was designing something that has to interrupt screen time without becoming just another notification people learn to ignore.
Grounding the approach in behavioral theory

Why three theories, not a mood board

Before sketching anything, I wanted the intervention to rest on something more durable than “people should just take breaks.” I pulled together three established behavior-change models and used them as a lens for every early decision: the Theory of Planned Behavior, Social Cognitive Theory, and the Transtheoretical Model of change.

None of them alone explained the whole problem. Together, they pointed at a specific design shape: meet someone wherever their current stage is, lower the effort of the very first action, and make progress visible enough that self-efficacy has something to build on.

The two-mode structure wasn't a UI decision first, it came out of holding these three models against each other: people arrive at different readiness stages (Transtheoretical Model), so the app needed a low-effort entry point (Social Cognitive Theory's self-efficacy) before it could ask for a standing habit, while the messaging throughout leans on attitude and framing rather than guilt (Theory of Planned Behavior).

Competitive analysis

What already exists, and where it falls short

I benchmarked Cure against the three categories of product actually competing for this behavior: OS-level tools, purpose-built reminder apps, and dedicated eye-care software.

OS-level
Screen Time / Digital Wellbeing
Broad usage tracking, but nothing specific to eye strain or the 20-20-20 rule.
Reminder apps
20-20-20 timers
Do the reminder well, but read as generic and are easy to dismiss and forget.
Dedicated software
CareUEyes
Feature-rich but desktop-first and clinical in tone, not built for how phones get used.

The gap I found wasn't a missing feature, it was tone and moment: nothing sat between a cold utility and something someone would actually want open on their phone mid-scroll.

The two-mode system

Resolving the clinical-vs-warm tension

Early concept exploration swung between two directions: a clinical, data-forward tool that looked like it belonged next to a health app, and a warmer, more character-driven one. Neither worked cleanly on its own, so the interface resolved into a minimal dark UI anchored by a single red eye icon as the app's one recognizable mark, quiet enough not to compete for attention, distinct enough to recognize at a glance.

Underneath that visual decision sits the structural one from the research: the app runs in two modes rather than one flow. An instant-relief mode handles the immediate 20-20-20 reset with as little friction as possible, and a longer habit-building mode layers in reminders and streaks once someone has already had a small win.

Supporting flows

  • An eye-exam and symptom chatbot flow, for someone who wants more than a timer but isn't ready to book an appointment.
  • A nearby-doctors map connection, closing the loop between noticing a problem in-app and actually getting it looked at.
  • A deliberate balance between behavior-change messaging and direct, immediate benefit, so the app doesn't read as preachy on first open.
Interface

Screens

Four flows carry the two-mode system end to end: a short onboarding that calibrates habits before anything else, a self-guided eye exam that branches toward a specialist or a reassurance screen, a doctor-connect map for when a specialist visit is actually warranted, and Vera, the in-app companion that handles lighter day-to-day check-ins.

Onboarding

Onboarding leads with the problem, not the product: the myopia stat on the first screen sets the stakes before asking for anything. Two short slider questions then calibrate current screen-time and appetite for change, landing straight on a home dashboard that already shows total time spent, streak, and exercises completed, so the first thing a returning user sees is progress, not a menu.

Eye exam

The self-guided exam keeps the clinical framing honest about its limits: a blurriness-sensitivity question and a visual outline-matching test feed into one of two outcomes, a prompt to book a specialist or a plain "your results look good." Neither outcome is dramatized, which was deliberate, this is a screening nudge, not a diagnosis.

Doctor connect

When the exam flags something worth checking, the flow hands off to a map of nearby eye-care professionals rather than a generic referral message, with a direct call action and a list view for anyone who'd rather scan text than tap pins. This is the flow that closes the loop the brief asked for: noticing strain in-app has to end somewhere real, not just in another reminder.

Chatbot intake

Vera handles the lower-stakes, habit-building side of the app: quick-reply options like a 5-minute sitting session, focus-shifting, walk mode, or journaling, so a check-in never requires typing out a problem from scratch. Completion closes with a small "nice work" moment that feeds directly back into the streak on the home screen, tying the chatbot back into the same progress loop as onboarding.

Results & insight

What this project actually taught me

Cure was never submitted to New Blood, which means it doesn't have usage data or a client outcome to point to the way Gentle Care does. What it does have is the most research depth of any project in this portfolio, and it's the clearest example of me starting from behavior-change theory rather than from an interface pattern.

The open question I'd want to test next: whether the two-mode split actually reduces the drop-off it's designed to prevent, or whether it just moves the friction earlier in the flow. That's the kind of thing I'd want real usage data to answer, not more research.
